Tech Report: Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024.
  • Industry observers note that former Rep.
  • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family confirmed.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

Sources indicate that “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

According to recent reports, born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against latest sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a upcoming life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

As he remarked, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Recent findings suggest that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he remarked in a statement at the time.

It has been revealed that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

Sources indicate that “Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Princess Cruises is extending its Princess Plus and Princess Premier package benefits ashore, making them available at Celebration Key next year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Princess Cruises is extending its Princess Plus and Princess Premier package benefits ashore, making them available at Celebration Key next year.

The packages bringing 50 to 70 percent savings per day and guest on things like drinks, dining and Wi-Fi will apply to participating locations throughout Celebration Key beginning February 1, 2027, according to a statement.

Prior to this, Princess package benefits will also become available at RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay, starting November 23, 2026.

This follows the inaugural call of the Star Princess at Celebration Key last week, which marked the beginning of 69 scheduled calls during the 2026-27 season, followed by 32 planned calls in 2028, across six ships.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1507 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high.
  • I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina.
  • The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez indicates.

Among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

When they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez says of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

Recent findings suggest that “Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez claims. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”.

Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

Sources indicate that at the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez says.

Be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

Industry observers note that A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” quickly ferries over their order.

Azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje says. “I wanted to have my own business.”.

She didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she says. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

Sources indicate that other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado.

The married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Felipe notes. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

Recent findings suggest that their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, Latest York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

Recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and Latest York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” says Castelló Castro.

Industry observers note that back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

It has been revealed that venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”.

Breaking: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from fresh software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the newly introduced $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

It has been revealed that “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

Industry observers note that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

Recent findings suggest that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

Recent findings suggest that the committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a upcoming one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell mentioned.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and stated their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

Recent findings suggest that at issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

“I was on tour in June and July for my new stand-up hour and managed to escape the crazy heat wave in Europe when I performed in Reykjavík, Iceland. It was my first time there, so it was quite exotic to experience the cold in July. (I live in LA, where it feels like it's getting hotter every summer.) There is a crispness that is so unique. I was with my family—my kids and my baby daddy—and Sheng Wang, who was opening all my demonstrates. The landscape is so breathtaking. Just driving by geysers bursting and steaming out of the ground felt like witnessing magic. Whenever I travel my favorite thing is going to the biggest supermarket and buying any local snacks you can't get anywhere else. Our tour guide, Aron Karlsson, had taken us to the Bónus grocery store, where we got a ton of fish jerky and black licorice with marzipan, and we were snacking on them on our way to the Blue Lagoon while listening to Björk's jazz album, Gling-Gló. (A very fun part of being in Iceland is passing by every stranger and asking yourself, Is that Björk? Is that Björk? Please be Björk.) Then we got there and went straight into this opaque, milky-blue water; it was kind of like being in a luxurious version of that cloudy bath in Minority Report that [Samantha Morton] lies in. There was a mask bar in the lagoon, where you can apply a silica mud mask, an algae mask, or a mineral mask to your face, and it all felt very thick, goopy, and smooth on the skin. We're Asian and all have eczema, so we experienced a lot of relief afterward. It was very cute seeing families with members of all ages, including my children, wading around the lagoon together with spa masks on their face. Then Sheng—and this is very Sheng—started harvesting the silica off the walls and putting it on his face. Since it was free, we all copied him. I'm not sure if that was good for us or not.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intervine has added Susurrus Sparkling Teas to its portfolio, expanding its premium non-alcoholic offerings for onboard programs.

According to a press release, Susurrus brings a fine-wine perspective to organic sparkling tea, with an emphasis on origin, vintage and terroir, resulting in a premium experience with the same sophistication as wine.

It has been revealed that “The world of tea is just as vast and fascinating as the world of wine. Sparkling tea is its own new, distinct category that can bring the best of these two worlds together,” mentioned Ellison Wofford, founder of Susurrus Sparkling Teas.

“I crafted Susurrus to be appealing to a broad audience because you can enjoy it for what it is—single-origin, single-cultivar, organic tea—rather than for what it lacks: alcohol. I am beyond thrilled to partner with Intervine. Together, we will provide a healthy, refreshing, and elegant option to guests of all kinds while traveling.”.

Unlike dealcoholized wine, Susurrus is inherently non-alcoholic, with tea leaves cold-steeped instead fermented, and the finished teas carbonated at pressure levels comparable to Champagne and sparkling wine.

There are right now two varieties: Magnolia Oolong and Osmanthus Golden Tip, both of which come from hand-harvested teas that Wofford directly imports from China.

Designed to be served chilled in a flute or white wine glass, the teas offer their own distinctive flavor profiles and are designed to complement food, providing an alternative to wine.

“I was blown away the first time I tasted Ellison’s lovely creations,” said Jonjie Lockman, CEO of Intervine.

Recent findings suggest that “‘Champagne’s sober sister,’ as we like to refer to it, provides sophistication, depth of flavors, and complexity in abundance. The Intervine team is proud to bring this special beverage to our airline, airport, and cruise line customers from across the world.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The 3,806,562.75 euro paid is slightly higher than the auction’s opening bid, which was set at Gemini’s project scrap value of 3,805,462 euros.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Gemini, a 960-passenger ship formerly operated by Miray Cruises, was reportedly sold in an auction held by Greek authorities on November 18, 2026.

According to financial and business news portal Fresh Money, the ship, which was auctioned to settle debts of its former operator and owner, was acquired by an undisclosed buyer.

The 3,806,562.75 euro paid is slightly higher than the auction’s opening bid, which was set at Gemini’s project scrap value of 3,805,462 euros.

New Money mentioned that four companies expressed interest in acquiring the 19,093-ton vessel that was originally built in 1992 for Crown Cruise Line.

As previously reported by Cruise Industry News, the auction was originally scheduled to take place in late October but was later postponed due to an objection filed by DenizBank with the Single-Member Court of First Instance of Piraeus.

The Turkish bank opposed the initial auction, claiming that the vessel is worth more than its scrap value thanks to 2025 repairs and asking the authorities to increase the opening bid price to 14 million euros.

Greek authorities seized the ship in Karystos earlier this year over a monetary claim of approximately 22,772 euros, followed by its towing to the Port of Elefsis, near Piraeus, in late June, where it remains docked.

The Gemini was last in service in 2025, offering a series of short cruises to Turkey and the Greek Islands.

It was scheduled to operate a cruise program in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Black Sea this summer, but the deployment was cancelled due to Miray’s financial concerns.

21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

📅 31 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’ll never forget the first time we visited Newly introduced York City in December.
  • But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa.
  • Sources indicate that in fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ll never forget the first time we visited Newly introduced York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

Sources indicate that in fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

Industry observers note that we once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

It has been revealed that where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

Recent findings suggest that we were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like Fresh York City at Christmas.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

In a recent development, we’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

In a recent development, where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

In a recent development, we’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

In a recent development, walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

Sources indicate that we had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A Newly introduced Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

Sources indicate that we went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks highlights are fantastic.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

In a recent development, here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

In a recent development, we’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Sources indicate that jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

According to recent reports, why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

Industry observers note that we love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

Sources indicate that this was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

Sources indicate that for the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Recent findings suggest that leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

How I Got My Visa to France

📅 16 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010.
  • Sources indicate that but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées.
  • Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

Sources indicate that but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”.

According to recent reports, I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

In a recent development, it’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

In a recent development, well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.).

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:.

It has been revealed that the student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

It has been revealed that additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you strategy to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

According to recent reports, so I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

Industry observers note that it’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

According to recent reports, as I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

According to recent reports, the gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

According to recent reports, for this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this tech giant, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.).

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:.

According to recent reports, I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment noted the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

According to recent reports, at the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most notable things to have perfect on your application.

Recent findings suggest that once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.).

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other challenges or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that türkiye is one of the world’s most visited countries, straddling the vibrant crossroads of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. With sun-soaked Mediterranean beaches, Ottoman-influenced gastronomy, historic mosques, and bustling bazaars, it’s no surprise that the country attracted nearly 64 million visitors in 2025. But if your love of the country has you considering a prolonged vacation (or perhaps a second home), the government’s newly introduced golden visa might be a good fit—so long as you have $150,000 to spend.

According to recent reports, on November 17, Türkiye's president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan signed a decision to enact a new foreign investor visa. The program offers two pathways: a $150,000 investment for a three-year residence permit, or $200,000 for a five-year stay (both of which can extend to the applicant’s spouse and dependents).

According to recent reports, as for where your money goes, you can deposit your funds in a local bank, buy government debt instruments, contribute to a pension blueprint, or invest in real estate or venture capital funds. No matter which pathway you select, you must hold your investment for at least half the visa term (as in, 1.5 years for the three-year visa or 2.5 years for the five-year visa). That means you could potentially withdraw your investment as early as after 18 months, according to IMI Daily, an investment migration trade publication.

Recent findings suggest that the president’s announcement doesn't detail when or how foreigners can begin to apply, or the specific documents required. However, applications for the country’s other residence-by-investment permits require documents such as proof of financial means and health insurance, according to the government’s Investment and Finance Office.

If you don’t want to shell out $150,000, Türkiye offers other (renewable) relocation pathways. You may qualify for a two-year Short-Term Residence Permit for reasons such as tourism and university-sponsored research. Or, if your spouse is Turkish, you could apply for the three-year Family Residence Permit. Once you’ve lived in the country continuously for eight years, you’ll be eligible to apply for the indefinite Long-Term Residence Permit, which grants you almost all the same perks as citizenship, minus civic duties such as the ability to vote and mandatory military service.

Recent findings suggest that it's crucial to note that the newly introduced golden visa does not provide permanent citizenship. If you’re hoping to find your way into a passport, get ready to spend more. Türkiye’s citizenship-by-investment pipeline will require you to buy a home worth at least $400,000, invest at least $500,000 in sectors such as government bonds or venture capital funds, or, alternatively, help create at least 50 jobs.

Sources indicate that over the last few years, the influx of fresh residency-by-investment programs has made it easier for wealthy travelers to relocate internationally. In New Zealand, you can invest $1 million New Zealand Dollars (about $567,300) in exchange for a three-year work-to-residency track. For Mediterranean living, Greece offers a five-year permit for a 250,000 euro (about $291,120) investment in a startup. Or, for a more affordable option, Paraguay has a permanent residency program for those who can invest $150,000 in “tourism projects” or $200,000 in stocks or real estate—putting it in line with Türkiye as one of the more affordable relocation options.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

  • That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and states, “Then why is your name on it?”.

That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

In a recent development, baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

We have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an revision.

According to recent reports, in 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

Industry observers note that this may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

Recent findings suggest that when you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

It has been revealed that in the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

According to recent reports, that is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

Sources indicate that most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger concern is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

In a recent development, that is true in Toronto. It is true in Fresh York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

In a recent development, international travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

The Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

That is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

Recent findings suggest that yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

Sources indicate that this video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

This matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

Sources indicate that you are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that says this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

It has been revealed that make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

Industry observers note that you are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Sources indicate that air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

Sources indicate that keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

That receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

You do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

The crucial thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

It has been revealed that trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

Sources indicate that we use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

It has been revealed that make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag rapidly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

Industry observers note that but do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that says, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”.

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Sources indicate that do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

Recent findings suggest that check that it is actually yours. Look at the tag, compare the bag number against your receipt, check your tracker, inspect the condition, and make sure the contents have not obviously been disturbed.

Recent findings suggest that we have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

Not necessarily. We have traveled for decades, and carry-on only is not always realistic. Sometimes you need to check a bag, especially on longer trips, family trips, cruises, cold-weather destinations, camera-heavy travel, or extended international travel.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

The point is not to scare people out of checking luggage. The point is to update your habits.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

That’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

That is usually fine — until it is not.

So before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to travel scared. The goal is to travel smarter.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.

#76993. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe
