    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Review: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres (Hyatt Inclusive)

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection.
    • Sources indicate that secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026.
    • Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection. My stay was almost exactly 24 hours and solo which is uncharacteristic at this destination resort. My experience will likely differ from other guests due to those factors.

    Sources indicate that secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026. It sits on a stretch of white-sand beach in Costa Mujeres, 12 miles north of Cancun. Cancun International Airport is the arrival airport. I could not confirm a single official transfer time from the property page. Tour listings commonly put the drive in a 30 to 45 minute range.

    Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico.

    Google Maps: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres.

    According to recent reports, hyatt is the best in the business at high end resort arrivals. I had given my name at the security gate and by the time I reached the lobby, the door to the vehicle was opened for me, I was greeted by name and a “welcome home”, a constant refrain throughout my stay. It’s a small thing and maybe cliché but it was effective. I was given a Globalist upgrade even though rules at all-inclusives differ from the rest of the chain. As my upgrade was in a Preferred room, I was brought into a private room at the front of the lobby where check-in was done for me.

    The lobby is an open-air room under an arched woven ceiling, with a direct view out to the ocean.

    The resort is spread across 10 buildings with 505 keys. Of those, 221 are Preferred Club keys with an elevated experience. My building (and others like it) had just five rooms on each floor and just five floors which made it feel boutique rather than massive. Every oceanfront room is Preferred Club, and so are the first two buildings on either side.

    The room views follow a simple rule by floor. Every first floor room is a swim-out, floors two through four are tropical view, and the fifth floor is ocean view or ocean front. That makes booking easy to reason through: if you want to step off your patio into the water, go low, and if you want the sea, go high.

    The walkways give a sense of grandeur and space. All of the flora is local, and in a touch I loved, the service rooms are named after the plants.

    Industry observers note that there are four pools, and each one has a unique characteristic. The Jungle pool is drinks only and hidden in the middle of the resort by trees. The Social pool runs activities throughout the day at this adults-only resort for those who want to participate. There is also an infinity pool on the edge of the beach, and then the Preferred Club pool for those staying in that category. These are separate from the first floor swim-outs.

    The spa (hydrotherapy is included for Preferred guests) featured an outdoor circuit that included both hot and cold plunge pools, amongst other therapeutic services.

    The Preferred Club pool was the most frequented, though some images below look more vacant due to rain that rolled through during my opportunity to collect media on my short stay.

    The gym is open to every guest from 6 AM to 8 PM, and it is outfitted with Technogym equipment.

    The spa is open 8 AM to 8 PM with 17 treatment cabins and a beauty salon, and hydrotherapy is included. That last part is the headline. The hydrotherapy space is ridiculous, easily the standout of the entire property for me, and it is the kind of amenity that would make me pick this resort over a competitor down the beach. There are indoor and outdoor showers as well.

    The men’s changing room featured private showers with an option for indoor or outdoor experiences.

    The theater seats 264 people and hosts cabaret and Mayan demonstrates. There are also pickleball courts, which I am starting to think should be required equipment at any resort that wants a younger crowd as well as padel for the European set (and growing American interest.).

    Secrets is an adults-only brand, and every room here comes with what the company calls Unlimited-Luxury. For a standard guest that means unlimited dining and top-shelf drinks, Wi-Fi, daytime activities and nightly entertainment, with tips and taxes included. Add 24-hour room service, a mini-bar refreshed daily (you can ask for just about anything you want in there), and pool and beach wait service for all guests.

    Recent findings suggest that the Preferred Club is an upgrade, and at this resort it is a big one because it owns the oceanfront. Secrets lists personalized check-in and check-out, afternoon hot and cold hors d’oeuvres, desserts and premium liquors, access to the Preferred Club lounge and beach bar, an upgraded mini-bar, upgraded bath amenities, butler service, Bali beds at the pool and beach reserved for club guests, and exclusive dining at the Preferred Club beach restaurant. Preferred also gives club guests exclusive access to an infinity pool and puts an oversized soaking tub on the terrace of the upgraded suites (at least with the oceanfronts).

    Recent findings suggest that I book a lot of Hyatt’s all-inclusives through Hyatt Privé rates, and this resort is one of 388 in the collection. Privé is Hyatt’s invitation-only program for travel advisors, so you only get the benefits when an approved advisor makes the booking, and the stay still earns World of Hyatt points and elite nights.

    Recent findings suggest that the all-inclusive version of Privé looks a lot different from a Park Hyatt booking. As I wrote when Hyatt’s all-inclusive resorts joined Privé, there is no room upgrade and no breakfast benefit, since every meal is already included. At this property, Privé guests receive a $100 resort credit per stay, a welcome amenity and letter, hydrotherapy access, and early check-in and late check-out based on availability.

    Elite status matters here more than at most all-inclusives. Under World of Hyatt’s terms, Globalists get the best room available at check-in, including rooms with club access, at the resort’s discretion. Explorists are eligible for upgrades too, but not to standard suites or club rooms. Travelers who have stayed at Secrets resorts as Globalists report being designated Preferred Club guests even when they did not land in a club building, which unlocks the lounge, pool and beach areas. This was my experience on all accounts at the resort. Late checkout is 2 PM for Explorists and 4 PM for Globalists, subject to availability at resorts. It was able to honor my request for a late check-out, I did not arrive early enough to request the early check-in. Hyatt waives resort fees on eligible paid rates (at least for now) and award nights for Globalists, and on award nights only for every other tier, and Globalists also get free parking on free nights though in 2028 Globalists will have to select this as a preference. One catch is that Suite Upgrade Awards cannot be used at Secrets resorts, so you cannot lock in a suite with one here.

    According to recent reports, weddings are massive business here. The courtyard outside the theater is the setting, with the sunset behind it, and the resort hosts lots of them. The resort disclosed its occupancy to me but it wasn’t clear if it was for public consumption. It was shockingly high especially for a Thursday in mid-November. Over the holidays or spring break all the hotels are full but this is a period where I would have expected a lull. Still, despite being extremely full, it never felt crowded.

    In a recent development, for meetings and groups, the convention space measures 9,800 square feet and splits into five sections. The boardroom was occupied at the time so I couldn’t include images of that.

    Industry observers note that restaurants can be booked in advance through the Hyatt Inclusive Collection app, which I wish more all-inclusives offered. Nobody wants to find out at 7 PM that the restaurant they wanted is full and through the app this can be done well in advance of a guest’s arrival. The dress code in the restaurants is resort casual, though the patio does not require slacks and closed toed shoes for men, shorts are acceptable outside.

    Industry observers note that the restaurants include: Portofino (Italian), Bordeaux (French), Himitsu (pan-Asian, with sushi and teppanyaki), Oceana (seafood in an open-air setting), Barefoot Grill (light lunch), Market Café (the international buffet, which I noted on site as the Marketplace), Seaside Grill (a poolside grill), and Coco Café. The bars on that list include Rendezvous in the lobby, Barracuda on the beach, a swim-up bar, a beach bar, and the Preferred Club beach bar and lounge bar. There’s also a Sports Bar and Lounge next to the theater.

    In a recent development, oceana is the seafood restaurant, set in an open-air dining room with woven pendant lamps, macrame hangings and a pebble mosaic floor. I chose this for my one dinner on property during my brief stay.

    I started with the lamb croquettes, which the menu serves with yogurt and sweet chili sauce, cashews, watercress and a pickled shallot salad, and the Iberian salad with fresh mozzarella, prosciutto, rucula, toasted pistachios, balsamic and roasted peach. A crusty loaf came with the meal.

    For a main I had the coconut shrimp, served with parsley orzo pasta, coconut sauce and parmesan crispy, and finished with the mango cheesecake, which the menu plates with vanilla cream and a mango compote with honey and basil.

    It has been revealed that market Café, the international buffet I noted as the Marketplace, serves breakfast until 11:30 AM. [TO CONFIRM: lunch and dinner service at Market Café].

    Industry observers note that seaside Grill hosts the Preferred Club à la carte breakfast. The official dining page indicates breakfast there is served for Preferred Club guests only. I tried a number of dishes for lunch to report to our fine audience.

    Rendezvous sits at the heart of the property with 360-degree access, so you can walk up to it from any direction.

    Preferred Club guests get their own bar at the beach, and the Preferred Club lounge also has an indoor lounge for when the sun gets to be too much.

    Recent findings suggest that my room was a Preferred Oceanfront King, a single open room with a king bed against a macrame headboard wall, rattan pendant lights, a ceiling fan, and a daybed sofa facing a marble bistro table. The balcony with jacuzzi looks straight over the beach. In the bathroom, a freestanding tub sits under a wood-slat ceiling beside a walk-in rain shower with a pebble floor and a bench. The double vanity has vessel sinks, round mirrors and a wave-textured wall, and the shower is stocked with Le Labo Bergamote 22 shampoo, conditioner and shower gel. Le Labo is a confirmed winner for me.

    I also had the chance to tour a master suites, all of which are oceanfront, and they are also available as swim-outs.

    Every first floor room is a swim-out, opening onto the pool.

    Industry observers note that secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an incredible resort that somehow felt small when you were in your building but big enough to have everything. For my stay, I used 45,000 points on a no-notice booking to offset a $1,300/night stay. I have seen rates from $560 for off-season which is without question worth it. I loved the property and I look forward to returning with more time and my wife, but the adults-only nature of the property will make it a harder stay for us to achieve.

    It has been revealed that what do you think? Have you stayed at Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres?

    #76916. Industry News: As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in Fresh Zealand Took My Breath Away

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1334 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in Fresh Zealand Took My Breath Away

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After taking the 17-hour Air Latest Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand.
    • I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown.
    • According to recent reports, I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After taking the 17-hour Air Latest Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand. I hopped around the North Island, relishing Auckland’s food scene, checking into the innovative Hotel Britomart, and visiting Wellington’s Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa. But when it came to the South Island, I realized the points of interest are far more spread out, with the massive Southern Alps to navigate through. The island has wide-open roads, but as an American conditioned to driving on the “wrong” side, I didn’t trust myself behind the wheel. So I turned to my favorite solution as a FOMO-fueled traveler who never wants to miss a highlight: scouring the GetYourGuide day-tour offerings to string together my ideal itinerary, a practice I’ve now participated in on all six continents.

    I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown. And while New Zealand’s natural beauty and the genuine Kiwi kindness made every experience enjoyable, the highlight was my grand finale: the Milford Sound Business Class small-group tour starting in Queenstown from a local operator called RealNZ. The round-trip 12-hour excursion brings guests in a glass-roof Mercedes Sprinter for stops along the iconic Milford Sound Road, then aboard a Milford Sound cruise through the fjord known as Piopiotahi in the Indigenous Māori language, which some consider to be the eighth wonder of the world.

    Check Availability at Get Your Guide.

    The wide-open views from the Sprinter van.

    According to recent reports, I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed. Each of the 14 black leather seats had a gray lambswool blanket, a plush green pillow, and a bottled shot of Manuka ginger Vitamin C boost juice. As a ginger shot addict who’s constantly searching for the best natural pick-me-up around the world, it was love at first sight.

    The long journey ahead—five hours each way—immediately shrank as our amicable guide provided context about where we were, explaining Milford Sound’s history, ecosystems, and Indigenous Māori connections. When all was quiet in the car, there was Starlink Wi-Fi to keep travelers entertained by their screens. After a quick refresher stop an hour in at the rural settlement of Garston, we reached the lakeside town of Te Anau, where one of its downtown shops served as our business class lounge.

    Sources indicate that here, the coffee order I’d requested at the top of the day was already waiting in a covered reusable mug with my name on it, alongside a plate of pastries. It wasn’t long before we entered Fiordland National Park, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Te Wahipounam. I looked up through the translucent roof as foliage from both sides of the road enveloped our van, winding through the gentle curves.

    Emerging through the Homer Tunnel, the writer stopped for this first glance of Milford Sound.

    Soon, the narrow road opened up, and we made our first stop at Eglinton Valley, an expansive glacier-carved flat where expansive fields of golden tussock grass are broken only by striking triangular peaks. Not long after were the aptly named Mirror Lakes, where the Earl Mountains are reflected near-perfectly in the glassy, still water; and Falls Creek, a craggy cascade that unfolds into a teal pond. During our stop at Monkey Creek, we spotted a couple of kea, the world’s only alpine parrots known for their playful behavior. Next, we drove through the Homer Tunnel, traveling less than a mile through the solid rock of Darran Mountain. Fittingly, our guide changed the soundtrack to the Jurassic Park theme as we dramatically emerged into Milford Sound at last.

    Sources indicate that as we descended through the twisty road into the Cleddau Valley, there were gasp-worthy sights at every turn. One minute we were heading toward a daunting granite mountain wall and the next we were looking out to the waters of the sound in the distance. After a quick stop at a bridge to catch a glimpse of Fiordland's highest peak, Mount Tūtuko, in the distance, we arrived at Milford Sound Visitor Terminal to board the MV Sinbad.

    A bridge across the Tūtoko River, which led to a view of Mount Tūtoko.

    The Cleddau Valley, with Milford Sound in the distance.

    Industry observers note that that's when the premium service was cranked up a notch. After I was welcomed with a glass of local Cloudy Bay wine, I was led to my own bean-shaped wooden table with two cushy swivel chairs on one side and a couch on the other, set against expansive windows that stretched overhead for views of the peaks and falls.

    A trio of dishes containing local ingredients, curated by chef Tom Hishon.

    Then came the five-course tasting menu. Already waiting was a seeded sourdough bun with whipped kelp butter, and it was followed by Fiordland wapiti (a local deer) bone broth soup. Next was a trio of artfully plated bite-sized dishes: paua (sea snail) with black garlic, a bite-sized fried ball made of titi (a local seabird), and roe from Mount Cook salmon. The penultimate dish was wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps plus smoked eel. It was all capped off with a “flat white”—an ice cream–topped dessert playing off the popular coffee drink.

    Sources indicate that between dishes, the captain of the MV Sinbad talked us through the highlights of Milford Sound, steering us up close to its plentiful cascades, including Sutherland Falls (1,904 feet tall), Lady Bowen Falls (531 feet), and Stirling Falls (508 feet). When he noted that Niagara Falls is only about 180 feet tall, I thought I misheard and went over to ask. But despite the massiveness of Milford Sound, the falls exuded a calmness that overshadowed their height.

    According to recent reports, the area is home to bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins, and humpback whales, and we caught a glimpse of a New Zealand fur seal lounging at Seal Rock. Throughout the two-hour cruise, the peaks—some craggy and pointy, others smooth and sloping—were a reassuring constant.

    Feeling rejuvenated thanks to both the power of Mother Nature’s beauty and the gourmet dining, we eventually returned to the van, where a generously sized bag of Marlborough Sea Salt Proper Crisps was waiting on my seat along with a Whittaker’s bar, New Zealand’s most famous chocolate. Of course, since it is business class, I also received a refreshing hand towel as I boarded.

    As we began the journey back to Queenstown, I gazed upward, soaking in the view from the car’s glass roof, with a contented smile. A rest stop later, I was so relaxed that I drifted off into a deep sleep. The next thing I knew, we were back in the city. We had spent 10 hours out of the 12-hour trip inside the van, but I hardly realized it thanks to all the luxurious touches at every turn. In this case, the journey was absolutely part of the destination.

    The Milford Sound Business Class tour launched in October 2025 as a joint operation between RealNZ and Altitude Tours. I originally saw the offering on GetYourGuide, my preferred tour booking platform for its flexible cancellation policies, but you can also book directly through the RealNZ website. The excursion starts at $383 per person for the business class tour, but a coach version is also available.

    The tour I took transferred from Queenstown, but RealNZ also offers the trip from Te Anau, as well as a self-drive experience. There’s also the option to book travel back to Queensland via a 45-minute flight in a fixed-wing aircraft for an additional cost, though it’s weather-dependent. For those seeking deeper immersion, there’s also an overnight cruise through Milford Sound, with the choice of private cabins with en suite bathrooms or shared bunk-style compartments.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific.
    • The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S.
    • French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a newly introduced interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    Recent findings suggest that southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    For French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    #76912. Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2.
    • My application was approved just before the June 30 deadline.
    • My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2. It also offered a faster track for Delta Diamond, Delta 360, AA Executive Platinum and Concierge Key members: earn 50 tiles by year-end and get Mosaic 4. That worked out to $5,000 in JetBlue flights or Paisly packages, or $50,000 on the JetBlue card, and a single Mint roundtrip to Europe could cover most of it. I already had AA Executive Platinum, so I didn’t need the status. I wanted it anyway. JetBlue was adding routes from my home airports, I fly to Boston, Fresh York and Fort Lauderdale often, and the United partnership raised the possibility of benefits on both sides.

    My application was approved just before the June 30 deadline. Some applicants waited up to six weeks for processing, though, and losing six weeks of a 12-week challenge is a real cost. JetBlue then added its 25-for-25 promotion on top. Visiting 25 destinations by year-end earned up to 350,000 TrueBlue points plus 25 years of Mosaic 1, which made a cheap, aggressive weekend of short hops look worth it. My strategy was to finish the challenge through spend and put the points toward transatlantic and Japan trips. My one worry at the time was whether JetBlue would treat these latest Mosaics well enough to keep them flying with it.

    My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW). I occasionally also fly from Fort Lauderdale or Miami when it makes sense. But Pittsburgh had just flights to Boston for some of last year, before adding Fort Lauderdale to fill the Spirit gap and then New York JFK competing with Delta, and more broadly to the New York market, United and American with more than enough flights. From Fort Myers, it’s Boston of JFK.

    I flew once to Boston on JetBlue but at the time, it had not yet debuted a domestic first class, a better seat selection included in my fare was the only real enhancement to the short flight of just over 80 minutes. I’ll cover other reasons why I wasn’t able to fly the carrier more, but given that I am not in Newly introduced York, Boston, or Fort Lauderdale full time, every flight I take has a connection and it’s not particularly on-the-way for me. For example, if heading south to Florida, Charlotte, Atlanta, or even Washington Dulles make more sense than Boston or New York but when heading west at all, Chicago, Houston, Dallas, and Denver are all obviously better options.

    Recent findings suggest that even to Europe, there’s not a material advantage with limited schedules and limited footprint on the continent. For trips to Paris given that I will have to connect anyway, I have more options on any other carrier through east coast hubs than with JetBlue on its metal not to mention partner networks.

    In a recent development, most recently, I had a flight to Cancun and with airport time, flight time and connections, it’s faster to fly out of Miami or Fort Lauderdale. But JetBlue had fewer flights for more money and far more miles than with American. Outside of the northeast corridor or based in South(east) Florida, I couldn’t make it make sense.

    Sources indicate that I’m heading to Europe for a meeting next week and I will finally have a chance to try Mint. This will constitute two of my longest flights with JetBlue ever. I haven’t heard many negative comments about JetBlue Mint, and I have high expectations. It’s hard to get excited about another American or United flight in business class solely because I have flown those so often and there’s little fresh there.

    It has been revealed that I’ll get a chance to try a reasonably long three-hour flight domestically to see how it differs from my prior JetBlue experience. Then, assuming flights are on time, I should have a chance to try the fresh BlueHouse, a first for me. Following that is a long haul flight in Mint and I am looking forward to the experience.

    According to recent reports, statistically, I can’t see a reason that I try for Mosaic again, but who knows? The experience could change what appears to be a clear analytical decision for me at this point.

    Industry observers note that one of the biggest reasons I secure status via flying/spending/staying is to redeem systemwide upgrades (or suite upgrades in the case of hotels.) I’ll fully admit that upon receiving approval for the challenge last year, I hadn’t even considered that Mint certificates would work differently than other upgrade certificates in the industry. One upgrade certificate is worth an upgrade (if available.) United uses “Plus Points” but it feels clearer that there will be some variability in what’s required to move between the cabins.

    Recent findings suggest that for this particular trip, JetBlue wanted two upgrade certificates in one direction, and four on another. Thankfully, I had taken the upgrade option every time I achieved a choice to select a benefit, but had I chosen something else assuming that I’d only need two Move to Mint certificates (as I would with American for example) I would have come up short.

    I covered how much spending is required to achieve top tier status and its associated benefits in recent posts. This was in response to United’s move to require $480,000 in annual spending (by credit card only) to achieve United 1K status. Assuming that along the way loyalty points are taken and annual Mosaic bonuses are applied to cardholders, JetBlue is above American at $225,000 in spend for Mosaic 4 vs. American’s net of $164,000 for Executive Platinum with just two systemwide upgrades, or $214,000 with six. The difference is that those six upgrades apply for the full-one-way on a single certificate.

    In a recent development, I spent time trying to figure out why one way charged four Move to Mint vs two and in the end, it didn’t really matter. I can nearly upgrade my entire family of four on American vs a single roundtrip for myself. For what it’s worth, the base cost was also more expensive with JetBlue than American for which I had upgrades available.

    I have the qualified business spend to earn Mosaic 4 every year, but the value of its perks aren’t even close to the rest of the market. And for what JetBlue expects in spend compared to what I could earn elsewhere is uncompetitive.

    And as a side note, the fixed rate of JetBlue points (about 1.4¢/each) is unimpressive but for most of the attempts I tried to use them throughout the year both domestically and internationally, they proved of little value. A lack of partners is much the same. I looked at a redemption in Mint on my flights to Europe and though I had more than 220,000, it was an insufficient balance for the simple roundtrip. For context, I took United a few years ago on miles and redeemed 160,000 roundtrip (this year was available at 176,000 roundtrip) and multiple times in the last 24 months on American at or around 115,000 roundtrip. Miles aren’t worth enough, they aren’t flexible enough, and there aren’t enough partners to fill gaps in the JetBlue map.

    It has been revealed that I had higher expectations for JetBlue based on the experiences of my peers. I think its equipment is excellent, but widespread first class availability is a necessity. The limited utility of Move to Mint certificates were the nail in the coffin and the usability of the miles didn’t help. But even then, I really want to love and fly JetBlue, and I am willing to go a little out of my way to use them. But I’m not willing to fly backwards for fewer flights at a higher cost.

    #76911. Industry News: Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Massive Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    Recent findings suggest that “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries mentioned. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for intends purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust latest majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Recent findings suggest that democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Without an revealed challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have stated they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Sources indicate that rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries mentioned Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Industry observers note that this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option. From early morning flights to daily office commutes, or even a packed Saturday afternoon at the farmers market, our editors are always relying on their favorite tote. The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. Whether you reach for a structured leather version to pack your essential items in or an oversized, canvas carryall for a day at the park, the functions of the right tote are infinite.

    Though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler. My favorite tote has been my everyday work bag for years, but it has also accompanied me on countless flights, weekend getaways, and last-minute happy hours. A reliable tote bag really can do it all. Keep reading to discover 15 of our editors' favorite tote bags and why we can’t live without them.

    It has been revealed that coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager. Though I still cherish that tiny bag, my most used Coach item is my leather tote. For years, the Nina Tote bag has been my reliable sidekick. I’ve had it for so long that Coach no longer produces it. On the bright side, the Maggie Tote bag is almost identical to mine and is just as practical. I have put my bag through anything and everything over the years, and there is very little wear and tear. The leather is structured and durable, yet flexible enough to fit everything I need without toppling over. With plenty of interior pockets, my necessities all have a place, so I never have to go digging through the bottom of my bag to find the right lip gloss. Not only do I love traveling with this tote, but it’s also my everyday work bag and my go-to for almost every kind of activity.

    According to recent reports, I've never really had a work bag that I truly loved until I tried this one from Cuyana. Aside from lugging it to and from the office each day, I use this tote as a personal item on the plane and brought it with me on a road trip to Acadia National Park, and have found it to be the ultimate travel companion. The built-in interior pocket is perfect for storing essentials you need to reach easily, like your passport, earbuds, or some petty cash, and since the bag can be snapped closed, you don't have to worry about anything flying out. —Jamie Spain, travel bookings editor.

I actually bring it to work with me every day—the laptop sleeve and spacious interior keep me organized on my way to and from the office. —Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor.

    I've received so many compliments on this gorgeous structured bag from Cuyana—it's been a great work bag, with plenty of space for my laptop, planner, Kindle, chargers, and other day-to-day essentials. I wasn't sure how well it would function as a personal item as there's not a zipper to fully close the bag, but on a flight to Aruba, I made use of the leather ties to keep items contained, and found it well-sized to slip under the seat in front of me, even with my toiletry bag and a sweatshirt stuffed inside. I'm also a major fan of the snap-to-close key leash, and the interior slips pockets and zipper pocket. —Madison Flager, commerce director.

    Recent findings suggest that the bag is perfect in the way a red apple sitting on a teacher’s desk is perfect. It’s classic, without ornament, the kind of thing that expresses its utility in its design. It’s both ubiquitous and aspirational, stirring up images of a dreamy East Coast: a white-sand, Nantucket beach; a shabby, wood-planked boathouse on the coast of Maine; a Gothic-inspired Ivy League campus. I've used it as a carry-on item, a beach tote, and as a weekender. Simply having it out on display in your home has the power to imbue your space with a charming, outdoorsy vibe. —Jessica Sulima, commerce writer.

    Baggu’s Nylon shoulder bag is more durable than its canvas tote bags but equally as stylish. It’s slightly slouchy, slightly structured, and comes in the signature Baggu colors and patterns. The adjustable quilted shoulder strap allows for a crossbody fit, a must-have for me when I’m commuting into the office or walking longer distances (nobody needs their laptop sliding off their shoulder onto the sidewalk). The zip closure and interior pockets are handy for organizing miscellaneous goodies and preventing spillage. Plus, the lightweight material can easily be flattened to fit into my suitcase. I find myself continuously reaching for this multipurpose tote on my way to the gym, office, farmers market, and airport. —Hannah Towey, associate editor.

    Just when I think I’ve run out of room, I haven’t. The expandable bottom of this Calpak laptop tote adds an extra four inches, allowing me to add last-minute essentials or souvenirs mid-trip. Like all products in the brand’s Luka collection, it’s made of a lightweight, ultra-soft, puffy exterior that makes carrying its handle easy. The material is also easy to clean—simply wipe away dirt or spills without a worry. Inside, there’s a padded 15" laptop sleeve, multiple side pockets, and a zippered section to keep smaller items organized. Another feature I love: There’s a zippered pocket on the outside that keeps my phone or passport secure, while still being easy to access. It’s a great tote for commuters and thanks to its luggage trolley sleeve, an ideal carry-on bag for travelers. —M.K.

    Industry observers note that as a shopping writer who is constantly running between the office, press previews, catch ups with friends and, of course, the airport, I need a bag with space for all the day’s exploits and then some. July’s Juliette Soft Work Tote is my perfect do-it-all companion. It’s beautiful—I’ve received multiple compliments on this bag as I’ve been whizzing around with it, and the divided interior is really clever. There’s a 14" laptop sleeve to keep tech protected—all the more crucial when you’re headed on a flight— and there’s also a dedicated water bottle holder too. It has a wide bottom so your lunchbox can go inside flat, plus a key leash to stop the rummage for your house keys. Brushed gold hardware and a buttery-soft faux leather exterior mean it looks effortlessly chic at after-work drinks, and when I'm off to the airport, the removable trolley sleeve slides over my suitcase handle so I can breeze through the terminal. It is my favorite desk-to-departure tote bag. —Charley Ward, commerce writer, Condé Nast Traveller UK.

    In a recent development, my Strathberry Kite is my most-used travel accessory. Not only do I use it for day-to-day tasks, it comes with me on almost every trip (the exception being adventure travel), and most recently carried me through trips to Lisbon and Istanbul, where I spent weekends catching up with friends and sightseeing. It's an ideal size for a laptop, should you wish to take it, but fits in plenty of other necessary items, too (like flip-flops or ballet flats after hours of strolling through cobbled streets). I love the walnut color and the soft, supple leather. I'm sure this will be a favorite of mine for years to come. —Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager.

    Industry observers note that when I first saw Parker Thatch offers its Jack Tote bag in this unique zebra and burgundy color combo, I knew it had to be mine. I never travel without animal print, and there was something about this colorway that felt perfectly understated yet maximalist. I found it online about a year ago, and it sold like hot cakes—and has been (devastatingly) sold out since. I received it as a sweet gift from my partner a few months ago, who had pre-ordered it to arrive right when it was back in stock. I've been using it as my go-to work bag ever since. It has an incredible amount of space and strength to carry all of my everyday essentials and then some—from my laptop and a book to makeup and toiletries. Because of its exterior fabric as hair-on cowhide, she just needs to be shielded from the rain a bit more than your average bag. If the design is calling your name on this bad boy, it’s well worth the splurge. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer.

    I love anything Longchamp, and this gorgeous beach tote from the brand is my cherry on top of any vacation outfit. It’s large enough to hold a full day’s worth of goodies (sunscreen! sweatshirt! beach read!), but fits on the shoulder with ease. Plus, the toggle on the front keeps things contained in the most Longchamp-esque way. —H.C.

    Sources indicate that after passing the gauntlet of a last-minute trip to the British Virgin Islands, I always keep the Foldie Travel Bag on me, whether it’s riding in my backpack during my daily commute or stuffed into my suitcase on longer hauls. The front pocket easily held my thick reading list and two Moleskine classic notebooks; the full 40 liters of space in the main compartment (with the expansion unzipped) fit a week’s worth of clothes, chargers for four different devices, and another bag filled with toiletry bottles, plus room to spare for souvenirs. Another perk: the two inner pockets and wet pocket proved useful in sorting out the bag’s increasingly chaotic contents. The luggage sleeve was a relieving bonus that allowed me to transfer the hefty weight of my zealous packing to my suitcase. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations.

    Industry observers note that I absolutely love this tote. Whether I’m wearing it to the office or while traveling, it fits everything I need. Plus, it comes with a separate removable pouch that I use even when I’m not wearing the bag. This slouchy bag is super durable and matches any outfit. —Pooja Nayyar, associate social media manager.

    Sentimentality may cloud my vision, for the tote in my possession belongs to my late grandmother. And when I tell you I was complimented frequently for it while in Italy, I mean I felt I needed to use the bag to beat back admirers waxing: “Wow, is Vera Bradley back?”; “Is it reversible?!”; “The textiles are so beautiful.” I often caught myself fantasizing about dumping it upside down to perform a “What’s in my bag” for nobody in particular—so capacious is the tote that I was needlessly carrying multiple novels within and rarely remembered to leave my toiletry kit on the hotel bathroom counter where it belonged. Handy pockets ringing the interior are just icing, and would have kept my passport safely inside had I ever been moved to act on the aforementioned dumping. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor.

    #76908. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (680 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    Sources indicate that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    It has been revealed that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    In a recent development, that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an notable part of it.”.

    It has been revealed that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” remarked Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley noted that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley noted. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very organization that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox noted in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    According to recent reports, “We require age checks for chat, place owners under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson noted. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    In a recent development, myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also remarked that Hawley’s fresh arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    #76907. Industry News: 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

    📅 26 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2655 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

    📅 26 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table.
    • According to recent reports, whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues.
    • When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table. The best winter vacation destinations offer comfortable temperatures, off-peak advantages, and festive happenings. On this list, you’ll find some of the usual suspects, from Punta Cana to the US Virgin Islands, as well as locales you might not have considered (far too often, travelers forget vibrant Marrakech is a shorter-haul Mediterranean option).

    According to recent reports, whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues. So, trade your snow boots for flip-flops and get to plotting your next escape.

    When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.

    If you’ve been looking for an excuse to finally book that trip to Hawaii, shoot for after the holiday rush, when flights get significantly cheaper. January might be the start of rainy season in Maui, but the showers are often short and localized; for the most part, you’ll enjoy sunshiny days with temperatures that hover in the low-80s. Humpback whales make their way from Alaska around this time, and you can spot the giant beauties from Papawai Point on Honoapiilani Highway, an overlook facing the ʻAuʻau Channel. If you’re not afraid of big waves, heavy north swells at this time of year make for excellent surfing, especially at Ho‘okipa Beach Park. The Road to Hana, a scenic and beautiful drive at any time of year, becomes especially lush in the winter after the rain has fallen, and you’ll likely avoid the crowds too. Along the way, hit up sites like the Twin Falls or the black sand beach at Waianapanapa State Park.

    It has been revealed that where to stay: A Condé Nast Traveler Triple Crown winner, Hāna-Maui Resort, a luxurious off-grid escape, is the pot of gold at the end of the Road to Hana, while Hotel Wailea offers an adults-only vibe on the southwestern coast. Though much humbler, Jimi Hendrix’s former gingerbread-style home, now available for rent on Airbnb, is also a fair contender for your home away from home, surrounded by all kinds of fruit trees and perfectly positioned for daily rainbows.

    When to go: December–JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees.

    It has been revealed that while you won’t be breaking a sweat in San Diego come December, it’s an excellent place to escape to around the holidays for festive fun in mild, mid-60-degree temperatures. The Parade of Lights is a classic seasonal event, when over 100 private boats get decked out in twinkling lights and sail around San Diego Bay (watch from spots like Shelter Island or Seaport Village on select nights in December). Between November and January, you can also enjoy ice skating without the chill at the Hotel del Coronado, where you’ll glide alongside the Pacific. They say San Diego sunsets are best in the winter, when the sun cuts a path closer to the horizon and there’s not as much coastal marine fog—one of the best places to catch one is Sunset Cliffs Natural Park on the Point Loma peninsula.

    Industry observers note that where to stay: La Valencia, otherwise known as the “Pink Lady” of La Jolla, is one of San Diego’s most iconic stays, and you might hear a seal or two barking in the distance. For unparalleled mountain views, consider this glass house overlooking Sweetwater Regional Park.

    When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 70–85 degrees.

    For a Caribbean escape with outdoor adventure, cultural festivals, and farm-to-table splendor, head to Puerto Rico. From December to March, you can take advantage of the dry season on the island, which means your days won’t be interrupted by sudden showers. Holiday festivities continue well beyond Christmas, from Three Kings Day on January 6—the oldest of these celebrations takes place in Juana Díaz, with a reenactment of the Magi on horseback—to the San Sebastian Street Festival, when the namesake street in Old San Juan is filled with art vendors, live music, and plenty of mofongo (January 21–24 this year). Winter is also a great time to explore El Yunque National Forest when it’s not shrouded in unbearable humidity—hike to La Coca Waterfall, take in the green canopy from Yokahú Tower, and keep an ear out for singing coquí frogs.

    Where to stay: For luxe accommodations just a 25-minute drive from El Yunque, look no further than Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, which coordinates guided treks with a strong emphasis on Indigenous history. Condado Ocean Club offers direct access to the beach, while this lakefront retreat near Cueva Ventana and Arecibo Observatory is ideal for couples seeking verdant views.

    When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees.

    In a recent development, another destination where US travelers can leave their passports at home, the US Virgin Islands are a quintessential Caribbean paradise. December through March is peak season, and there are plenty of reasons why—no rain, calm seas, and temperatures that hover between 77 and 85 degrees, to name a few. St. Croix, the largest of the USVI’s three main islands, is defined by the white sands of Rainbow Beach, as well as its Danish ancestry, which you can explore at colonial-era sites like Fort Frederik and Fort Christiansvaern. St. John is filled with all kinds of natural wonders; take the Underwater Snorkel Trail at Trunk Bay to peer at parrotfish, or set off on the three-mile Reef Bay Trail to hike among pre-Columbian petroglyphs painted by Taíno Indians. St. Thomas is a bustling port with cosmopolitan charm, and you’d be well advised to sample a few conch fritters at Gladys' Café. Whichever island you choose, clear skies and turquoise waters await.

    Where to stay: One of Traveler’s favorite private island resorts (and the only one in the US Virgin Islands), Lovango Resort and Beach Club is located across St. John’s Caneel Bay and offers all kinds of eco-chic accommodations, from wooden treehouses to explorer-style tents. The Westin St. Thomas is set right in front of the harbor, with a stellar spa worth traveling for. For something a bit more intimate, this light-filled, two-bedroom cottage is just a five-minute walk away from Cruz Beach.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees.

    Recent findings suggest that while temperatures do drop in Marrakech during the winter—the peaks of the Atlas Mountains will be blanketed in snow—you’ll see far more sun than in certain parts of the US; plus, it’s all the more reason to enjoy a steamy hammam. Winter is a great time to explore the city's popular sites with thinner crowds: comb through the medina’s bustling souks for fragrant spices and a pair of babouche slippers, take in the cobalt blue buildings at the Jardin Majorelle, or learn about one of France’s most legendary fashion designers at the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Keep an eye out for the dates of the Marrakech International Film Festival, which takes place between the months of November and December—this year it falls from November 20 to 28, and features 76 films from 39 countries.

    Where to stay: Traveler contributor Jordan Lippe-McGraw is a massive fan of this family-friendly villa, with a heated pool, hammam, and cinema room. A Triple Crown winner, La Mamounia is the city’s grand dame. As global features director Erin Florio puts it, “Every inch of this palatial property has been hyper-considered to make the guest feel as though they have arrived in some regal estate of an Arabian kingdom.” At the Royal Mansour, all riads come with 24/7 access to a private butler.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–90 degrees.

    The Arenal Volcano looms over Costa Rica’s La Fortuna region, heating its natural springs, and there’s a greater chance you’ll see it without cloud cover in the winter. For travelers seeking a combo of adventure and relaxation, La Fortuna (about a three-hour drive from San José) is well-suited for both. Hike through cooled lava fields at Arenal Volcano National Park or swim around La Fortuna Waterfall, then take advantage of nature’s healing powers at Tabacón Thermal Resort and Spa. For a truly memorable experience, book a tour with Arenal Horse Tours and ride your steed straight into the Arenal River for a refreshing dip.

    Where to stay: While Tabacón is perhaps the most iconic resort in the area, The Springs Resort & Spa is another great option, boasting two dozen hot springs, pools, and waterfalls spread across the 65-acre property. If you’re looking for something more intimate, this forest cabin features a private spring-fed pool, rain shower, and marked hiking trails—a one-of-a-kind off-grid retreat.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.

    Though small, this Central American country offers a diversity of experiences, whether you want to take it slow in a charming fishing village or ascend latest heights in the jungle. Perhaps the most popular destination on Belize’s tourism map, Ambergris Caye is a departure point for the country’s barrier reef—though just south of Ambergris Caye, Caye Caulker provides a nice alternative. While on the car-free island, book a tour with Ragga Sail Adventures for a half-day snorkel through Hol Chan Marine Reserve, the oldest marine reserve in the country. Further south in Punta Gorda, you’ll find rugged adventures and a strong sense of Mayan culture. Here, you’ll have access to several offshore cayes (Belize has hundreds of these small islands, brimming with marine life), from Snake Cayes to Sapodilla Cayes Marine Reserve; if you prefer jungle, take a boat tour through the Monkey River, or hike to the waterfall at Rio Blanco National Park. And be sure to explore the surrounding Toledo District for Mayan ruins, like the Lubaantun, which dates back to 700–900 AD and is also an excellent site for birdwatching.

    In a recent development, where to stay: Nestled within the Belizean rainforest, Copal Tree Lodge’s jungle suites will make you feel as though you’re suspended among the trees. Wake up to the sounds of monkeys every morning, then take a farm tour around the surrounding property, where you’ll discover how cacao, vanilla, and sugar cane grow. Over in San Pedro, Alaia Belize is your luxury option, just 600 yards away from the barrier reef, while this tiny home will make you feel as though you’re vacationing in a fairy tale.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80 degrees.

    According to recent reports, december through April is peak vacation time in Punta Cana, when the rainy season has subsided and there’s not a cloud in the sky. With average highs in the 80s and average lows in the 70s, you’re likely to experience perfect weather during your stay. Come February, you’ve got a good chance of spotting some humpback whales if you cast your eyes off the coast of the Península de Samaná, where they typically pass through until April. The country also celebrates Independence Day in February—on the 27th, to be exact. Visit around that time, and you’re bound to run into a Carnaval parade or bachata dance circle. With the Cordillera Oriental mountain range looming in the background and a selection of cenotes around town—from Hoyo Azul to Hoyo Claro—mountain buggy excursions and diving adventures await even in the winter.

    Where to stay: The W Punta Cana redefines the all-inclusive resort as we know it with top-tier dining and some of the largest rooms in the country. Hyatt Vivid Punta Cana, which just opened its doors in August 2026, is another upscale all-inclusive in the area, boasting swim-out suites and a chic speakeasy. If you’ve got kids in tow but still want to experience the height of luxury, Eden Roc Cap Cana is a consistent Readers' Choice Awards winner. For a villa the whole family will enjoy, this eight-bedroom Airbnb in Tortuga Bay comes with a private pool.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 70 degrees.

    Recent findings suggest that another prime location for whale watching, Baja California’s southern tip sees the migration of humpback and gray whales between the months of December and April (you might even elect to swim with whale sharks, too, which roam around the nearby Bay of La Paz around this time). You’ll have just missed the rainy season in November, making way for sunny, 70-degree beach days and not-too-chilly evenings. The creative town of Todos Santos boasts a number of art galleries to pop into, like Galeria de Todos Santos and La Sonrisa de la Muerte, while the Sierra de la Laguna mountains are home to stunning trails and swimming holes. If you’re a surfer, Playa Los Cerritos and Playa San Pedro offer some of Mexico’s best waves.

    Where to stay: Todos Santos is home to a number of cutting-edge boutique hotels. Hotel San Cristobal, with its vibrant interiors and delectably fresh seafood, perfectly embodies the bohemian vibes of this tiny surf town. Paradero Todos Santos, located on a five-and-a-half-acre farm, is designed around outdoor adventure: Pick the “Unbound” option, and surfing, hiking, and biking experiences will all be included in the nightly fare. If you prefer to go the rental route, this little bungalow is set among farmland in Pescadero, with its own private rooftop.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 75 degrees.

    In a recent development, miami is a good idea any time of year, but December through February is considered the dry season, promising temperatures in the mid-70s. Two key events pop up this time of year: Art Basel Miami, in December (4–6, this year), and the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, in February (running the 25–28 in 2027). But there’s always something to do in the Magic City, whether that’s taking a peek into the Pérez Art Museum, spending money in the Design District, or having a stroll through the Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.

    Industry observers note that where to stay: To embrace the happy-go-lucky spirit of the locals, check in to the Goodtime Hotel and sip on a Purple Reign cocktail (co-owner Pharrell’s favorite drink) at the rooftop pool club. If you’d like to tap into the city’s Art Deco architectural history, stay at The Moore, where you’ll be close to Wynwood and Downtown Miami. This dreamy loft in Collins Park, just a short walk to the beach, is a good bet too.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees.

    Recent findings suggest that depending on where you’re coming from, Cape Town might be a little out of the way. But the US's winter is their summer, and with that comes sunny days and a dry, Mediterranean-like climate. Around mid-January, tourists start to flee and kids return to school, making popular attractions more accessible. Take a cable car (or hike, if you’re feeling bold) up to the famous Table Mountain, or drive to Boulders Beach, which boasts one of the last colonies of African penguins in the world. There are plenty of opportunities to engage with some art, as well, from the contemporary galleries at Zeitz MOCAA to the rainbow houses of the Bo-Kaap Museum. And if you’re feeling especially adventurous, you can treat Cape Town as a jumping-off point for the famed Garden Route road trip.

    Where to stay: For views of both Table Mountain and the V&A Waterfront, stay at the Silo Hotel, housed in a former grain silo and famous for its maximalist interior design. For something a little more off-the-beaten-path, Ellerman House is an Edwardian mansion turned boutique hotel situated in the exclusive Bantry Bay area. And if it's privacy you're after, this three-bedroom bungalow in St. James features a private hot tub and covered deck with gorgeous sea views.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.
    • The carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from Latest York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027.
    • American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

    The carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from Latest York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

    American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

    Recent findings suggest that israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and New York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

    American also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

    The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

    Sources indicate that “American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava mentioned in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

    Israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. Fresh York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

    American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (282 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.
    • It has been revealed that seymour will step down on Dec.
    • Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    It has been revealed that seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

    Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    In a recent development, gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A new reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be confirmed in December.

    “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    #76902. Tech Report: How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples
